findings.description: The Jasypt password is just reverse(busId + version), both stored in plaintext in the same row and hard-coded in SecurityConstants ("jot","v1"), so the password is always "1vtoj". Anyone with read access to main.sec, main.sec_aud (Envers copies the value) or any DB dump/backup can decrypt the HMAC key and forge JWTs for any user, including admins. Because the entity is @Audited, rotated-out keys also remain recoverable in sec_aud after the documented 'delete the row' rotation.
findings.title: JWT signing secret 'encryption' key is derived solely from public, constant row fields
findings.verification: Confirmed from code: derivePassword uses only busId/version; docs/deployment/secrets-reference.md shows JwtSecretBootstrapRunner is the production provisioning path for (v1, jot).

findings.description: The existence check calls secretService.fetchSecret, which only loads the entity and never calls getSecretBytes, so DECR_ERROR/BLANK_SECRET can never be raised here. A broken (v1, jot) row (e.g. hand-written SQL with the wrong Jasypt password) is logged as 'skip_existing SUCCESS' and the app boots, then fails every request when JwtConfiguration.getSecretKey decrypts it, contrary to the javadoc's promise to stop the boot.
findings.title: Bootstrap runner's 'fail on corrupt/undecryptable row' guard never fires
findings.verification: Confirmed by reading SecretService.fetchSecret (no decryption) versus the javadoc's 'Fails startup loudly' bullet.

findings.description: JwtSecretService and JwtConfiguration resolve the key with findOneByVersionAndBusId, which ignores EntityStatus. Setting the row to INACTIVE to revoke a compromised key, or creating it with createInactiveSecret, has no effect: it keeps signing and verifying tokens. The bootstrap runner likewise treats an inactive row as 'present' and skips creation, while fetchLatestActiveSecretAsBytes would report KEY_NOT_FOUND for the same data.
findings.title: JWT secret is fetched without regard to status; INACTIVE secrets are still used for signing
findings.verification: Confirm whether any operational procedure deactivates secrets via status; the code path itself is confirmed.

findings.description: The first active secret fetched per busId is stored in secretMap forever. createActiveSecret never evicts it, and nothing else does either, so a newer active secret is never returned by this instance. Separate instances also cache different values. The size check followed by put is also non-atomic. The method currently has no callers in src/main, so this is latent.
findings.title: Latest-active-secret cache is never invalidated, so rotation is ignored until restart
findings.verification: Grep shows no callers of fetchLatestActiveSecretAsBytes in src/main; becomes live once a caller is added.

findings.description: The error-context maps are built with Map.of(..., VERSION, version, BUS_ID, busId) before validation, and Map.of rejects null values. So fetchSecret(null, x) or createActiveSecret(x, null) throws an NPE and never the BLANK_VERSION/BLANK_BUS_ID SecException. Secret.derivePassword has the same problem for a null field: it throws an NPE instead of BLANK_BUS_ID_OR_VERSION. Callers that catch SecException (like the bootstrap runner) do not handle it.
findings.title: Null busId/version causes NullPointerException from Map.of instead of the intended SecException
findings.verification: Java's Map.of throws NPE on null values; confirmed by reading the code.

findings.description: When the ThreadLocal is empty (e.g. code running outside SecurityAdviceFilter, async threads, schedulers), getKey silently returns new byte[0] instead of throwing. A caller that feeds this into an HMAC without a length check would sign or verify tokens with an empty key, and such tokens can be forged. No current caller exists in src/main, so this is latent.
findings.title: JwtSecretProvider.getKey returns an empty key instead of failing when no secret is bound
findings.verification: Grep shows no callers of JwtSecretProvider.getKey in src/main; risk depends on future callers.

findings.description: The Secret entity is cached, but each getSecretKey call builds a new BasicTextEncryptor and runs a full PBEWithMD5AndDES decrypt (1000 key-derivation iterations) to get the key. Each token sign or verify pays this CPU cost, so a burst of authenticated requests multiplies it.
findings.title: Signing key is PBE-decrypted on every getSecretKey call
findings.verification: Profile JwtConfiguration.getSecretKey under load to quantify.
